summary: A discussion of how to make connections between minicomputer-based terminals and a TIP more reliable. The existing protocol sends one character at a time with no error control, assuming a human can spot errors. That assumption fails for faster or automated terminals, so the author raises ways to detect and correct errors.

plainLanguage.summary: The TIP-terminal protocol sent characters without error checks and assumed a person would spot mistakes. RFC 230 explains why automated terminals and remote links need a machine-based way to detect errors.

questions: why does a tip terminal connection need error control
subtitle: Why automated or remote terminals need error control beyond character-by-character transmission.

tldr.problem: The existing TIP-terminal protocol had no error control and relied on a person to notice errors, an assumption that fails for fast, remote or automated systems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC discusses adding block-oriented transmission and error control, with the control loop located either at the TIP or at the serving host.
tldr.outcome: It presents implementation options for more reliable terminal links, not a finalized protocol.

today: RFC 230 is a discussion of reliable terminal links published in September 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: When Human Error Checking Fails
sections.content:
The existing TIP-terminal protocol was character-oriented and did not provide error control. It assumed interactive use, where a person could notice corrupted characters while reading the exchange.

The RFC says this assumption may fail on faster links, remote connections, terminals with their own logic, process-control or laboratory systems, and remote batch terminals where a human is not in the communication loop.
sections.plainLanguage: A person may notice an error while reading a terminal. Automated systems and fast or remote connections cannot rely on someone checking every character.

sections.title: Block-Oriented Error Control
sections.content:
The author suggests adding blocks of data with delimiting and error-control information on top of the existing character protocol. Blocks could be multiples of one character, so the underlying link would still send start and stop bits for each character.

The RFC notes this would not use the channel as efficiently as synchronous block communication, but considers the loss not substantial in the described setting.
sections.plainLanguage: Characters can be grouped into blocks that include a way to detect errors and mark block boundaries. The existing character link can still carry those blocks.

sections.title: Where to Place the Control Loop
sections.content:
One approach would add software and block buffering to the TIP so error control ends at the TIP-terminal connection. The author notes that this could place too much load on the TIP.

Another approach would put the far end of the control loop in the serving host, either in an application or system software. The host software might also support host-to-host error control, though the embedded character format could reduce efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Error checking could run in the TIP or in the serving host. The TIP approach adds work to the TIP; the host approach could be reused but may be less efficient.
